title: Ojibwe on Bird's War Road
summary: In June 1780 about a hundred Odawa and Ojibwe warriors joined Capt. Henry Bird’s British invasion that took Ruddle’s and Martin’s stations in Kentucky.
bodyMarkdown:
The [Ojibwe](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ojibwe) call themselves Anishinaabeg, often translated "Original People." Their homelands lie around the Great Lakes, far north of Kentucky. With the [Odawa](https://grokipedia.com/page/Odawa) and the [Potawatomi](/stories/potawatomi-fire-keepers-and-the-ohio-valley-wars/), they formed the alliance known as the Council of the Three Fires. The Odawa name comes from the Anishinaabe word *adaawe*, "to trade," and Odawa traders linked networks from the St. Lawrence to the Mississippi.

Both nations had already fought colonial expansion. In 1763 the Odawa leader Obwandiyag, known as Pontiac, built a coalition that besieged British forts, including Detroit. Seventeen years later, in the American Revolution, Odawa and Ojibwe warriors fought alongside the British against American settlers in Kentucky.

## A British plan

In the spring of 1780, Britain planned four attacks on Spanish and American posts in the West. At Detroit, Major Arent DePeyster chose Captain Henry Bird to capture the American fort at the [Falls of the Ohio](/stories/falls-of-the-ohio/). The plan answered [George Rogers Clark](/stories/george-rogers-clark/)'s capture of Illinois posts in 1778 and 1779.

[Bird's force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird%27s_invasion_of_Kentucky) left Detroit on May 25, 1780, with 150 regulars and militia, two artillery guns and about 100 Odawa and Ojibwe. At the mouth of the Great Miami, Alexander McKee of the British Indian Department joined them with 600 warriors, mostly Shawnee, led by [Blue Jacket](/stories/blue-jacket-weyapiersenwah/).

## The Licking River stations

The warriors believed, wrongly, that Clark had returned to the Falls. They insisted on striking the isolated Licking River settlements instead, and the expedition turned there. On June 22, Ruddle's Station surrendered when the settlers saw a six-pounder cannon being moved into place. The warriors ignored the surrender terms and took most of the people captive.

The death toll is disputed. A claim made in 1843 put it at twenty, while the station's leader, Isaac Ruddle, later reported three deaths. Martin's Station surrendered without a shot, and none of its captives were harmed. Bird refused to go on to Bryan's Station and Lexington, citing short supplies and the many prisoners.

## The road north

Bird's men escorted about 150 prisoners to Detroit. The warriors held 200 to 250 more. Most were brought to Detroit and ransomed, but some were killed on the way, in what historian Russell Mahan called a death march. Enslaved people taken in the raid were treated as plunder, and some were given to Bird, McKee and Simon Girty.

News of the raid led settlers to abandon several isolated Kentucky stations. In August, Clark struck back, defeating the Shawnee at Piqua and destroying the Shawnee towns of Chillicothe and Piqua.

## Kentucky today

The Odawa and Ojibwe homelands lay far to the north, and their nations endure there. Ojibwe communities live on more than 20 reservations in the U.S. Great Lakes states and on many reserves in Canada. Odawa nations include the Little Traverse Bay Bands in Michigan and the Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma. Some of the Kentucky captives, for their part, stayed in Canada for good after the war.
